title: When the Lantern Turns
premise: In 1899, Astrid Crane drives for celebrated suffragist Miriam Vale, quietly reading the letters she delivers and learning more about the movement's secrets than anyone suspects. When a census taker's probing questions expose a hidden identity in Miriam's household, Astrid discovers the movement is harboring a fugitive — her own brother, presumed dead for a crime he may not have committed. As the constables close in and the movement's leaders weigh sacrificing him for the cause, Astrid must decide whom to save: her brother, her mentor, or the truth itself. She secures the last berth on a steamer bound for Canada on New Year's Eve, but the choice of who takes it will cost her everything she thought she was.
about_author: Edmund Ishikawa is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing suffrage-era correspondence in regional collections. He writes historical fiction about the invisible people who kept history's famous moments moving.

chapters.title: The Question Behind the Question
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. A census taker arrives at Miriam Vale's townhouse and asks about the young man in the attic photograph — a man Astrid has never seen. She deflects, but the encounter rattles her. Emotional beat: the uneasy thrill of realizing her careful invisibility has a crack in it.

chapters.title: Letters I Wasn't Meant to Read
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV, with a flashback to how she began reading the mail. A coded letter arrives referencing 'the boy at Harrow Lane,' and Astrid recognizes her brother Tomas's handwriting — the brother who died, officially, six years ago. Emotional beat: grief colliding with disbelief.

chapters.title: Harrow Lane
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. She follows the letter's address and finds Tomas living under a false name, working as a printer for the movement. He swears he didn't commit the arson that killed a factory foreman. Emotional beat: the vertigo of a reunion that cannot be spoken aloud.

chapters.title: What Miriam Knows
chapters.summary: Miriam's POV. Miriam reveals she has known Tomas's identity for two years and sheltered him as a debt to Astrid's late mother, a fellow suffragist. But the census inquiry has drawn a constable's attention, and Miriam must weigh the cause against the boy. Emotional beat: loyalty strained against political survival.

chapters.title: The Constable's Patience
chapters.summary: Alternating Astrid and Constable Dreever's POV. Dreever, methodical and courteous, begins visiting the townhouse weekly, asking harmless questions that are never harmless. Astrid starts feeding him small true things to hide the large false one. Emotional beat: the seductive danger of lying well.

chapters.title: A Berth for the Century
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. The movement arranges passage for a witness in a separate trial — one berth on a steamer leaving December 31. Tomas needs it; so does a young organizer whose testimony could win the vote in two provinces. There is only one berth. Emotional beat: the sick arithmetic of sacrifice.

chapters.title: The Vote in the Kitchen
chapters.summary: Miriam, Astrid, and the movement's inner circle argue over the berth. Miriam's POV dominates: she argues for the witness, the cause, the future. Astrid hears her mother's memory being spent like currency. Emotional beat: justice revealed as something with a body count.

chapters.title: Confession at the Print Shop
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. He confesses to Astrid that he was at the factory that night — not setting the fire, but letting it burn, because the foreman had destroyed evidence that would have freed their mother. Emotional beat: the collapse of the one clean truth Astrid was standing on.

chapters.title: When the Lantern Turns
chapters.summary: Climax. Astrid's POV. Dreever arrives on New Year's Eve with a warrant. Astrid drives Tomas toward the docks through the celebrating crowds, then makes her choice: she puts the witness on the steamer and turns the carriage toward the constabulary, trading Tomas's escape for a public confession that exposes the real arsonist — a factory owner. Emotional beat: terror transfigured into resolve.

chapters.title: The Last Letter
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV, epilogue, spring 1900. Tomas awaits a retrial with the owner's conviction secured; the movement wins its vote, owing its victory to the witness Astrid saved. Miriam offers her a position of real trust, and Astrid, for the first time, delivers a letter unread. Emotional beat: quiet, hard-won peace — identity chosen, not assigned.
